divergent selection for IGF-I in cattle resulted in a 20 ng/mL difference in serum IGF-I concentrations in progeny of selected animals.
divergent selection for IGF-I concentration has been effective in Angus beef cattle, but that the genetic correlations of IGF-I with growth, carcass, and reproductive performance traits are small.

the effects of divergent selection for IGF-I concentration and the effects of season of calving and sex on the expression of this trait in Angus beef cattle.
the genetic control of IGF-I expression and its role in the regulation of growth and reproduction in cattle.
the effects of divergent selection for IGF-I concentration, season, sex, and age of dam on IGF-I concentrations in serum of Angus cattle.

IGF-I concentrations are affected by season, sex, and diet.

the effects of season, sex, age of dam, and diet on IGF-I concentrations were confounded and that the only significant factor affecting IGF-I expression was the selection line to which the calf belonged.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
selection for IGF-I has been very effective in the Angus population and that IGF-I is a good predictor of growth and carcass merit.
selection for IGF-I is possible, but it is not a panacea.
selection for increased IGF-I concentration is effective and that the response is heritable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IGF-1 is a very heritable trait in Angus cattle.
the genetic correlation between IGF-1 and growth traits is not high enough to justify using the trait as a selection index.
